result:
I wake up to the sound of the radiator clicking off. It’s 6:42 and the light is that thin, blue-white winter kind that makes the room look like it’s been rinsed. I lie there for a minute with my eyes open because if I close them I’ll fall back in and then I’ll be late for the thing I don’t really want to do but have already decided to do. The ceiling has a faint water stain I’ve been meaning to look at for months. It looks like a continent. It looks like a hand. It looks like nothing if I stop trying.

I get up and the floor is cold against my feet. I always forget slippers until the second step. Coffee is already an idea before it’s a drink. The kettle takes forever. I watch the little bubbles form and climb. I think about how much of my life is spent watching things heat up. Water, people, arguments. The smell hits when I pour and it’s the only honest part of the morning.

The apartment smells like old books and laundry. I open the window a crack even though it’s cold because the air in here gets thick overnight, like it’s been breathing the same thoughts. The building across the street is having scaffolding put up. There are two men up there in yellow vests, eating sandwiches. One of them is reading a newspaper. The paper flaps. I wonder if they can see me.

I make toast and stand there while it browns, watching the color move across the surface. It’s a little violent how quickly it goes from pale to dark. I think about deadlines, and how they are just toasters with a timer. If you leave things in too long they burn, if you take them out too early they’re sad.

My phone is on the counter. I pick it up and put it down again. It’s vibrating in my pocket already. I don’t check. There are three kinds of messages I get in the morning: people who need something, people who want to know I’m okay, and automated reminders to be a better human. I want to be the kind of person who answers immediately. I am not that person yet.

I’m thinking about the word “whatever.” It’s a surrender and a permission slip at the same time. Whatever comes to you. It’s an invitation to be sloppy, to be honest, to be unedited. I’ve spent so much time editing myself that the unedited version feels obscene, like showing up without pants. But the pants are also uncomfortable. They chafe.

There’s a plant on the sill. It’s a pothos I rescued from a grocery store in March. It was drooping and half dead. I talked to it. I know that sounds ridiculous but plants respond to consistent care and I’ve been consistent with it, maybe more consistent than I’ve been with people. It has new leaves now, little heart-shaped things that unfurl slowly. I don’t know what to call that kind of patience.

I think about my father when he was alive and how he would drink his coffee black and stand at the sink with the window open, just watching the street. He never said much in the mornings. I used to think he was bored. Now I think he was listening. Maybe I’m listening now. The radiator clicked again. A car alarm went off two blocks down and stopped itself.

I have a meeting at nine about a project I’m not sure I believe in. That’s the second layer of the day: the thing I have to do, and the story I tell myself about why I have to do it. The story changes depending on how much sleep I got. Today the story is that I’m learning. Tomorrow it might be that I’m trapped. Both can be true.

I wash my mug. The water is hot on my hands. I like the feeling. It’s a clean, sharp sensation. I think about all the small pleasures I’ve trained myself not to notice because noticing feels indulgent. The way light catches dust. The way a good pen makes a line. The way someone laughs at exactly the right second.

I’m not sure what I’m waiting for. Some people wait for a sign. I think I’m waiting for permission to not have everything figured out. Maybe this is it. A prompt with a word limit and no direction. Write whatever comes to you. That’s all.

The toast is getting cold. The coffee is cooling too fast. I sit down at the table and open a notebook that’s half full of half-finished lists and doodles. I start writing because the alternative is scrolling, and scrolling is just someone else’s whatever.

It’s funny how the mind fills a blank page with the same stuff it fills a full one. Worries, memories, to-do lists, a random lyric from 2008. I let it come. I don’t judge it. The hand moves. The words come out clumsy and then a little clearer.

The sun is higher now. The blue-white has turned to yellow. The men on the scaffolding are gone. The plant is still there. The stain on the ceiling is still a continent. I’m still here, in the middle of it, with cold feet and warm hands and a cup that’s finally the right temperature.

I think that’s enough for now.
